common_name: Fooled Me Daylily (Lavender Extended-Bloom Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Fooled Me is a heavy rebloomer that benefits from a spring feeding to fuel repeat flushes of bloom through summer.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, watering deeply during dry spells to sustain its extended rebloom cycles. Fooled Me is a tetraploid cultivar hybridized by Patrick Stamile and introduced in 1994, bearing lavender-purple, ruffled flowers with a lime-green throat that hold open into the evening and sometimes a second day, an unusual trait for a daylily. It flushes repeatedly from early summer into fall rather than concentrating bloom into one period, making it one of the more reliable modern rebloomers for extending daylily color in the border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; the eye pattern stays crisper when foliage is kept evergreen and undamaged by hard freezes.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving light afternoon shade where summers are extremely hot to preserve flower substance. Spacecoast Starburst is part of the Florida-bred Spacecoast series developed by Anna Pulver and is prized for its bold gold flowers marked with a radiating, starburst-shaped eye zone in deeper rose-red around the throat. Its evergreen foliage and vigorous branching produce a long midsummer bloom season with high bud count per scape. It combines well with solid-colored daylilies, which set off its patterned blooms.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the bright red color and gold ruffled edge hold their intensity best with consistent moisture and protection from the most intense afternoon sun in hot regions.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, watering regularly through the growing season to support heavy bud counts. Christmas Is, hybridized by Elizabeth Salter and introduced in 1997, produces vivid red, ruffled flowers edged in gold with a small green throat, and was awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2001 for its exceptional garden performance. Its strong scapes hold blooms well above tetraploid-vigor foliage, and it branches heavily for a long midseason display. It remains one of the most widely grown red-and-gold daylilies in cultivation today.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society - Stout Silver Medal

common_name: Court Magician Daylily (Deep Purple Daylily with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; deep purple daylilies like Court Magician hold their richest color when given morning sun and light relief from the hottest afternoon rays.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, though a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates helps preserve its saturated color. Court Magician bears deep royal-purple flowers with ruffled edges and a contrasting chartreuse-green throat, a striking combination that has kept it a popular choice among purple daylily enthusiasts since its introduction in the 1980s. It is a vigorous, floriferous grower that multiplies readily into full clumps within a few seasons. Pair it with pale yellow or cream daylilies to make the purple tone pop in the border.

common_name: Siloam Bo Peep Daylily (Miniature Pink Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; as a compact miniature, Siloam Bo Peep is well suited to edging, rock gardens, and small containers.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every few years to maintain dense flowering. Siloam Bo Peep is part of the celebrated Siloam series of miniature and small-flowered daylilies bred by Pauline Henry of Siloam Springs, Arkansas, and was registered in 1981. It produces soft pink, rounded flowers with a rose-red eye zone and green throat on compact, grassy clumps that stay tidy through the season. Its dwarf habit and dependable bloom make it a favorite for the front of the perennial border.

common_name: Startle Daylily (Cream and Rose Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; regular moisture and a balanced spring feeding help maximize scape and bud count.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, watering consistently during bud development for the fullest flower display. Startle, a tetraploid hybridized by Patrick Stamile, bears near-white to pale pink flowers accented by a wide rose-red eye band and a matching picotee edge, giving the bloom strong contrast and definition from a distance. It carries high bud counts on well-branched scapes, extending its bloom season well beyond many older eyed cultivars. Its crisp color pattern makes it a strong focal point among softer pastel daylilies.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chicago Sunrise, like other Chicago-series daylilies, performs best with full sun exposure for strongest color and bud count.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, dividing every three to four years as clumps become crowded. Chicago Sunrise belongs to the influential Chicago series of hardy daylilies bred in Illinois, and produces warm golden-orange flowers with a deeper orange throat blush on sturdy, well-branched scapes. It is a dependable midseason bloomer valued for its cold hardiness and vigorous, fast-multiplying clumps, characteristics shared across the Chicago-series introductions. Its bright, sunny color reads well from a distance, making it useful as a mass planting or border accent.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, moist soil in full sun; the compact habit makes Picasso well suited to containers and small garden beds.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, feeding monthly during the growing season to sustain repeat bloom. Picasso is a dwarf canna cultivar with plain green foliage and bright yellow flowers freckled with irregular red-orange spots reminiscent of an artist's spatter pattern, giving it a distinctive, playful look. Its compact height compared to standard tall cannas makes it a popular choice for mixed containers, patio pots, and the front of tropical-themed borders. In zones below its hardiness range, dig and store rhizomes indoors over winter after the first killing frost blackens the foliage.

common_name: Feuerzauber Canna (Fire Magic Heirloom Red Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; this tall heirloom cultivar benefits from staking or a sheltered location in windy sites.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, watering generously through the season since cannas are heavy drinkers. Feuerzauber, German for 'fire magic,' is a classic Crozy-type canna dating to the early twentieth-century German breeding tradition, bearing broad green leaves and large, vivid orange-red flowers on tall, sturdy stalks. Its heirloom status and old-fashioned Crozy flower form, rounder and less orchid-like than modern hybrids, have kept it in circulation among collectors of historic garden plants. It makes a bold back-of-border or pond-edge planting where its height and color can be appreciated from a distance.

common_name: Tropical Rose Canna (Compact Seed-Grown Pink Canna)

planting.note: Set out transplants or plant rhizomes after the last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; the compact Tropical series blooms earlier and stays shorter than traditional tall cannas.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, feeding regularly to support its extended bloom season. Tropical Rose is a member of the compact Tropical series of cannas, bred as uniform, early-flowering seed-grown hybrids that brought the All-America Selections award to the series in 1992 for blooming reliably in its first year from seed. It bears clear rose-pink flowers over plain green foliage on a shorter, bushier plant than heirloom tall cannas, making it useful for mass bedding displays and mixed containers. Deadhead spent flower stalks to keep new blooms coming through summer and fall.

common_name: Konigin Charlotte Canna (Queen Charlotte Heirloom Red-and-Gold Canna)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after the last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; this vigorous heirloom cultivar naturalizes readily and benefits from division every few years to control clump size.

directions: Plant rhizomes 3-4 inches deep in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun, dividing clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor. Konigin Charlotte, or Queen Charlotte, is a Crozy-type canna dating to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, producing large red flowers edged in bright golden yellow above broad green leaves. Its classic bicolor blooms and tall, robust habit have made it a long-standing heirloom favorite for bold summer color at the back of the border or along fences. Like other tall cannas it is a heavy feeder and drinker, rewarding rich soil and regular water with the tallest, most floriferous growth.
